candidates.speaker: client
candidates.text: The new contract is for $850, with milestones organized by scene. I’ve also uploaded a revised script to the shared google folder; it has only a few small changes from the previous version. Since you don’t need to create the text cards, I’ll handle those myself. That may leave a little extra in funds for fine-tuning, although we’ll have to see how things go. Please let me know if anything is unclear. Thanks!

candidates.speaker: client
candidates.text: To reduce costs, storyboards are often kept in black and white; the final video, however, must be in full color.

candidates.speaker: client
candidates.text: Use a 9:16 aspect ratio with a vertical orientation.

candidates.speaker: client
candidates.text: I hadn’t realized this limitation existed. Do low-angle shots automatically have lower resolution, while higher-angle shots can achieve better resolution? I’m fine with changing the shot angles whenever doing so improves the quality of the set images.

candidates.speaker: client
candidates.text: Let’s secure all the other required material before spending time on the opening aerial establishing shot. I still want that shot, but it has a lower priority than everything else we need.

candidates.speaker: client
candidates.text: My set images don’t seem high quality enough, and I hadn’t realized we would be limited to their existing resolution. Would generating new set images to use as starting frames improve the quality, and is that worth doing? I’m fine with that approach if it would help.

candidates.speaker: client
candidates.text: New sets are fine with me, provided they remain stylistically on point and consistent across the shots. If possible, though, I want to keep the long wide shots that open the sequence.

candidates.speaker: client
candidates.text: The framing moves from wide in the first set to mid in the second, then closer in the third.

candidates.speaker: client
candidates.text: Sorry—the confusion came from my using "set" in more than one sense. There are three PAIRS of images, and each pair contains 1 shot of Kestrel and 1 shot of Red Fern. In framing order, the first two images are long/wide, the second two images are mid, and the third pair is closer, showing them from the waist up.

candidates.speaker: client
candidates.text: Compared with my originals, these revised sets are much more similar to one another.

candidates.speaker: client
candidates.text: Overall, these look good, but a few small issues remain. The bridge behind Kestrel at his waste is badly placed; please remove it along with the bridge just above his head. To prevent the lower bridges from interfering, leave only the one upper bridge in the Kestrel images. The character shadows are also missing—can you restore them without changing anything else? Thanks for sticking with it!

candidates.speaker: client
candidates.text: The character shadows visible in earlier renders are absent from these renders.

candidates.speaker: client
candidates.text: Please pause for now while I compile a list of any other changes before you do more work, so we don’t waste effort. Because I’m traveling today, I can only send it tomorrow or the day after.

candidates.speaker: client
candidates.text: While the other work is paused, you could keep going on SQ4 if you want, using my notes from yesterday about the energy blast.

candidates.speaker: client
candidates.text: Before work resumes, please allow me a day. During that time, I’ll capture any and all changes and write a detailed description of the remaining shots in SQ4.

candidates.speaker: client
candidates.text: The script already specified the shot angles I wanted and explicitly noted that the storyboard angles were wrong. If you followed only the storyboard reel rather than the script, that explains why we misunderstood each other. Since I can’t reliably create images with the right angles to demonstrate them in the reel, what alternative process would work for you? How should I communicate each angle so you can render the shot correctly?

candidates.speaker: client
candidates.text: Getting both the character details and the style I prefer has also been difficult. If I provide two images—one for character details and one for style—could you try generating an image that combines both aspects?

candidates.speaker: client
candidates.text: To clarify, although I mentioned presenting still frames as a digital comic book, I want to attempt the animation first. I’ll fall back to the digital comic book with still frames only if the animation produces poor results or proves too difficult or expensive.

candidates.speaker: client
candidates.text: Let’s hold off on moving forward until we finesse the character style a bit. It keeps drifting, and I’ve struggled to keep it precise. Red Fern and Blue Lantern are close to the target; Kestrel is furthest away because he feels too clean, too simple, and too polished. What I want instead is more of a raw graffiti aesthetic. Could you do a quick pass applying that style to all three of them and send me the results?

candidates.speaker: client
candidates.text: More attitude comes through in this reference: it’s darker and rougher, with stronger sketch energy.

candidates.speaker: client
candidates.text: This is my favorite of the three because of his detail and features, so use it as the target if you need one.

candidates.speaker: client
candidates.text: What additional funds would you require for just one attempt at altering the style of all three characters, followed by recreating the frames as we currently have them?

candidates.speaker: client
candidates.text: Since the character details are already dialed in and we have a target style, I had hoped this would be easier. Ah, okay—I'll try it on my own instead.
